title: Is SRP always the right call?
summary: A confident "no, and here's the counter-case" reads far stronger than parroting the principle back at the interviewer.

slides.markdown:
This is a trap question dressed as a definitional one. "Is SRP always right" is really asking: **can you push back on a principle you clearly know, with a concrete counter-case?** Candidates who answer "yes, always split responsibilities" sound like they've memorized a rule they've never applied to a real codebase.

The strong shape: state the principle, name a real situation where following it literally makes things worse, then give the actual rule of thumb you use instead.

Ask **"always as in every codebase size, or always as in every team size?"** — the two constraints point at different counter-cases. A three-person startup and a five-hundred-engineer org hit SRP's costs and benefits at very different points, and picking the right counter-case depends on which one the interviewer means.

This question also buys a beat to line up the counter-case you're about to give, rather than answering reflexively.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: principle, counter-case, rule of thumb
slides.markdown:
State it plainly: **no.** SRP reduces the blast radius of change, but splitting has its own cost — more files to navigate, more indirection to trace through, more test setup per piece. Below a certain size or change-rate, that cost exceeds the benefit.

The rule of thumb: split when you can name two *actual*, currently-happening reasons this class changes for different actors; don't split preemptively for a reason that hasn't shown up yet.

Cross-link: **[SRP: Single Responsibility](srp-single-responsibility)**.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: split into four pieces, now harder to navigate
slides.markdown:
```python
class UserValidator: ...
class UserNormalizer: ...
class UserPersister: ...
class UserNotifier: ...

# calling code now needs all four, wired together, to do one conceptual thing
validator, normalizer = UserValidator(), UserNormalizer()
persister, notifier = UserPersister(), UserNotifier()
def create_user(data):
    validator.check(data)
    clean = normalizer.normalize(data)
    persister.save(clean)
    notifier.notify(clean)
```
Four classes for what reads, at this size, as one cohesive "create a user" operation — a reviewer now has to open four files to understand one flow.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: kept as one cohesive unit, and why that's right here
slides.markdown:
```python
class UserOnboarding:
    def create(self, data):
        self._check(data)
        clean = self._normalize(data)
        self._save(clean)
        self._notify(clean)
```
Same behavior, one file, one thing to open to understand "how a user gets created." It's the right call while all four steps change together, for the same reason, at the same time — split it only once one step starts changing independently of the others (say, notification channels multiply while validation stays fixed).

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how small is too small — what's your smell test?
slides.markdown:
The smell test: if you can't describe two of a class's methods as serving genuinely different *actors* or *reasons to change*, it's not too small — it's appropriately sized. "This changes when validation rules change" and "this changes when the DB schema changes" are two real actors; "this changes when we rename a variable" isn't a second actor at all.

A useful gut check: would splitting this let two different people work on two pieces without stepping on each other? If not yet, it's premature.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how does this interact with cohesion?
slides.markdown:
SRP and cohesion pull the same direction until they don't: SRP asks "does this have one reason to change," cohesion asks "do these methods actually belong together." A class can satisfy SRP narrowly (it has exactly one reason to change) while still failing cohesion if its methods don't share data or purpose beyond that.

The practical read: over-applying SRP without checking cohesion produces classes that are individually single-purpose but collectively scattered, forcing callers to juggle many small pieces to do one coherent thing.

Cross-link: **[coupling and cohesion](coupling-and-cohesion)**.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: does team size change where you draw this line?
slides.markdown:
Yes, directly. A solo developer or a two-person team pays the navigation cost of splitting with little payoff, since nobody's stepping on anyone else inside the same class. A fifty-engineer org gets real value from the same split — it lets separate teams own separate pieces, deploy independently, and avoid merge conflicts on a shared file.

The honest answer names this explicitly: "I'd draw the line differently for a two-person team than a fifty-engineer org," rather than giving one universal threshold.

**Weak belief:** SRP should be applied maximally, always, because more granular classes are inherently better design.

**Why it's weak:** it ignores the real cost side of the trade-off entirely — more files, more indirection, more test setup — and reads as reciting a rule rather than having applied it.

**Correct model:** split when the benefit (isolating actual, currently-happening change) exceeds the navigation cost; not before.

slides.sectionTitle: Wrong answer: "SRP is overrated, keep everything in one class"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** the opposite overcorrection — since SRP has costs, it should be mostly ignored and classes should stay large by default.

**Why it's wrong:** this throws away the real, well-documented benefit SRP provides once a class genuinely serves multiple actors — merge conflicts, blast-radius risk, and untestable god-classes are real costs of *not* splitting.

**Correct model:** the right answer isn't picking a side, it's naming the threshold where the trade-off flips.

"No, not always. SRP reduces blast radius, but splitting isn't free — more files, more indirection, more test setup. Below a certain size, or while several steps still change together for the same reason, one cohesive class is the right call. I split once I can name two *actual* actors driving change independently — not preemptively for a reason that hasn't shown up yet. Team size shifts where this line sits too: a two-person team pays the split's cost with little payoff; a fifty-engineer org gets real value from the same split."

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: split vs cohesive-one-class, at this team's size
slides.markdown:
| | Split into four classes | One cohesive class |
|---|---|---|
| Navigation cost | Higher — four files for one flow | Lower — one file, one story |
| Merge-conflict risk | Lower — separate files | Higher if multiple people touch it |
| Right for | Multiple actors changing it independently | One actor, steps that change together |
| Team size it suits | Larger, multiple owners | Solo or small team |

How to decide: check whether two people are actually stepping on each other in this class today — not whether they theoretically could.
